477.title: He wept over it (Luke 19:41–44)
477.hook: Jesus weeps over Jerusalem: if thou hadst known the things for peace
477.howItsDone: Pilgrims in the Holy Land celebrate Mass at the Dominus Flevit chapel on the Mount of Olives, facing the old city, and Catholics pray for peace in Jerusalem and in places at war in the prayers of the faithful.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ten servants with one pound each, and one who buried his in a napkin. Your line was trade with it.

On the western slope of the Mount of Olives there's a small church shaped like a teardrop. It was built in the 1950s, and its name is Latin: Dominus Flevit, the Lord wept. Behind the altar, a big window looks straight across the valley at the old city of Jerusalem, so the priest at Mass faces the view. On the front of the altar is a mosaic of a hen gathering her chicks. The church marks one moment. Jesus has come down the hill on a colt, with crowds shouting praise. And then, at the sight of the city, he stops.
screen: `A CHURCH SHAPED LIKE A TEAR.` → `DOMINUS FLEVIT: THE LORD WEPT.` → `A WINDOW FACING THE CITY.`

segments.voice: It's what Christians call Palm Sunday. Crowds are spreading their cloaks on the road, shouting blessed is the king who comes in the name of the Lord. In the middle of that joyful procession, Luke says: "And when he drew near, seeing the city, he wept over it." Luke's word means to weep aloud, to sob. Then he speaks to the city: "If thou also hadst known, and that in this thy day, the things that are to thy peace; but now they are hidden from thy eyes." There's a play on words in it. Many people heard the name Jerusalem as containing shalom, peace. The city of peace hasn't recognized what makes for peace. Then he grieves over what's coming: enemies will surround the city, and not leave a stone upon a stone, because thou hast not known the time of thy visitation. Christians later read these words in light of what happened about forty years after: in the year 70 the Roman army besieged Jerusalem and destroyed the Temple, and many thousands died. Hear it the way Jesus says it. He doesn't gloat. He doesn't curse. He weeps, the way you'd weep over a child running toward a road. Remember the hen: how often would I have gathered thy children. It's the same love. Catholics hear in this a God who isn't distant from the suffering of cities. Before the stones fall, someone stood on a hill and cried for them by name.

Let yourself feel something for the people there, without needing to fix it or take a side. If you pray, ask for the things that make for peace there; if you don't, hold them in your attention with care.
Visitation. The time Jerusalem didn't know, when Jesus looked at the city in the middle of a joyful procession and sobbed. Today's word.
Your line: the things for peace. Grief, not gloating, from the hill. Day four hundred seventy-seven, done.

478.title: Not one stone (Luke 21:1–6)
478.hook: the widow's mites, then the Temple's beauty and its end
478.tomorrow: Do this for a commemoration of me
478.howItsDone: Catholics bring offerings to the altar at the offertory of every Mass, and parishes sometimes point to the widow's mite when they speak of giving: not the size of the gift, but how much of yourself is in it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the visitation: Jesus wept over Jerusalem in the middle of the palms. Your line was the things for peace.

Two scenes sit side by side in Luke, within six verses, both in the Temple. In the first, Jesus watches rich people casting their gifts into the treasury, a steady clink of coins. Then a poor widow drops in two brass mites. In the second, some people are admiring the building itself: its goodly stones, and the gifts that adorn it. A tiny gift, and a vast one. Which one lasts?
screen: `THE CLINK OF RICH PEOPLE'S COINS.` → `TWO BRASS MITES.` → `GOODLY STONES AND GIFTS.`

segments.voice: First the widow. The Douay calls her coins two brass mites; Luke's Greek calls them lepta, small coins. Jesus says: "Verily I say to you, that this poor widow hath cast in more than they all." The others gave out of their abundance. She gave out of her want, all the living that she had. Jesus doesn't measure the amount. He measures what was left after. Then, a moment later, people are praising the Temple. They had reason. This was the Temple Herod the Great had rebuilt, and Josephus, who saw it, says that from a distance it looked like a snowy mountain, white stone and gold. And Jesus says: "The days will come in which there shall not be left a stone upon a stone that shall not be thrown down." Yesterday he said it weeping, on the hill. Today he says it standing among the stones themselves. Put the two scenes together and they ask one question: what lasts? The great stones, admired by the crowd, did not. The two coins, noticed by Jesus, are still read aloud wherever this Gospel is read. Luke isn't saying buildings are bad. Catholics build cathedrals. He's asking where a heart rests. Stones, however beautiful, fall. A gift of the whole self is remembered.

segments.voice: Make a quiet list of what you're proud of, or worried about keeping, a house, a title, a reputation, a bank balance, and hold each one a moment as what it is: good, and temporary. Then bring to mind something that lasts, a love you've given, a kindness someone still remembers, faith if you have it, and rest there. If you pray, offer God something small and whole, like the widow's two coins.

Your line: what lasts. Two brass mites outlasted all the Temple's goodly stones. See you tomorrow.

479.title: Do this for a commemoration of me (Luke 22:14–20)
479.hook: Luke's words of institution, the root of the Mass
479.howItsDone: At every Mass the priest repeats the words of institution over the bread and wine, and Catholics kneel or bow at the elevation; on Holy Thursday the Church celebrates the Mass of the Lord's Supper, remembering this night.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mites: a widow's two small coins, and the Temple's great stones. Your line was what lasts.

The words a priest says over the bread at every Mass were first spoken, Luke says, in an upper room in Jerusalem. Luke even tells how the room was found. Jesus sends Peter and John ahead to prepare the Passover: follow a man carrying a pitcher of water into a house. The owner shows them a large upper room, furnished, just as Jesus said. The hour comes, and he sits down at table with the twelve apostles.
screen: `THE WORDS SAID AT EVERY MASS.` → `A LARGE UPPER ROOM, FURNISHED.` → `THE HOUR COMES.`

segments.voice: Luke begins with longing. Jesus says: "With desire I have desired to eat this pasch with you, before I suffer." The doubled phrase means: I have wanted this so much. Then a detail Luke records: two cups. Early in the meal Jesus takes a cup, gives thanks, and tells them to share it; he won't drink again of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom comes. Some readers connect this with the cups of wine at the Passover meal. Then the bread: "And taking bread, he gave thanks, and brake; and gave to them, saying: This is my body, which is given for you. Do this for a commemoration of me." And after supper, the second cup: "This is the chalice, the new testament in my blood, which shall be shed for you." Commemoration, in the Greek, is anamnesis. It isn't nostalgia, like looking at an old photo. The Passover command already speaks this way: Exodus tells each parent to explain the feast as what the Lord did for me, when I came out of Egypt. Remembering, there, makes the saving event present. Catholics believe that at Mass the one sacrifice of Christ is made present, not repeated, and that the bread and wine become his body and blood, which the Church calls transubstantiation. The Council of Trent also taught that with the words do this, Christ made the apostles priests. Other Christians understand these words differently; many Protestants see the supper as a memorial and a meal of faith. All start from this same table and this same command. Not believe this, or understand this, first. Do this.

segments.voice: Picture your next meal: the table, the plate, who'll be there, or that you'll be alone. Then picture, gently, that upper room: thirteen people, bread, a cup, a man who knew what was coming and still gave thanks. If you pray, give thanks the way he did; if you don't, simply remember that night and the people at it.

Your line: do this. A memory that makes the past present again. Good to see you today.

480.title: As one that serveth (Luke 22:24–27)
480.hook: at the supper they argue about greatness; he says I am among you as one that serves
480.carry: servant of the servants of God
480.howItsDone: Every Catholic priest and bishop is first ordained a deacon, and the Holy Thursday Mass of the Lord's Supper provides for the priest to wash the feet of members of the congregation, in memory of Christ serving at the Last Supper.

segments.voice: Yesterday, anamnesis: bread and cup in the upper room, memory made present. Your line was do this.

In Luke, the very next thing after the bread and the cup is an argument. Jesus has just said this is my body, given for you. He has just said one of them will betray him. And at that same table the apostles fall to arguing about which of them is the greater. A family bickering over the good chair at a hospital bedside. Mark and Matthew tell of a similar quarrel earlier, on the road; Luke sets it here, at the Last Supper.
screen: `RIGHT AFTER THE BREAD AND CUP.` → `WHICH OF US IS THE GREATER?` → `LUKE SETS IT AT THE SUPPER.`

segments.voice: Luke says: "And there was also a strife amongst them, which of them should seem to be the greater." Jesus doesn't scold them for wanting to matter. He redraws what mattering means. The kings of the nations lord it over people, he says, and those in power like to be called benefactors. "But you not so." Let the greater among you become as the younger, and the leader as one who serves. Then a simple question about the room they're in: who's greater, the one reclining at table or the one serving? At any dinner, the one at table. "But I am in the midst of you, as he that serveth." Present tense. Right now, at this table. The Greek word is diakonon, the one who waits on tables, from the same family as the word deacon. The Catholic Church builds this into its own shape. Every priest and bishop is first ordained a deacon, a servant, and that service is meant never to wear off. Pope Gregory the Great called himself servant of the servants of God, servus servorum Dei, and popes still use the title at the head of official letters. A title doesn't guarantee anyone lives up to it. It names the standard Jesus set the night before he died: greatness measured by service.

segments.voice: Picture the rooms you'll be in today, home, work, a bus, a store, and find one small job nobody wants: dishes in the sink, a full trash bag, a tired parent, a coworker drowning in a task. Picture yourself doing it quietly, without announcing it or waiting for thanks. If you pray, offer it as service.
Diakonon. The Greek word behind serveth: the one who waits on tables, Jesus' answer to his apostles' argument at the Last Supper. Today's word.

481.title: Drops of blood (Luke 22:39–46)
481.hook: only Luke tells of the angel and the sweat like drops of blood
481.howItsDone: Catholics pray the Agony in the Garden as the first sorrowful mystery of the rosary, and some keep a holy hour of prayer before the Blessed Sacrament, especially on Holy Thursday night.

segments.voice: Yesterday, diakonon: the apostles argued over greatness, and Jesus was among them as one who serves. Your line was servant of the servants of God.

It's late, and the supper is over. Jesus goes out to the Mount of Olives, to a place Luke says he went as he was accustomed. Somewhere he'd prayed before. A chair by a window, a corner of a church, a walk taken when something is too heavy: some people keep a place like that. He tells the disciples to pray that they don't enter into temptation. Then he goes on a little further, about a stone's throw, and kneels down.
screen: `OUT OF THE CITY, AFTER SUPPER.` → `A PLACE HE WENT AS ACCUSTOMED.` → `A STONE'S THROW FURTHER.`

segments.voice: He prays: "Father, if thou wilt, remove this chalice from me: but yet not my will, but thine be done." The chalice is the cup of suffering ahead. He asks honestly for it to pass, then hands the decision over. Then Luke gives two details no other Gospel has: "And there appeared to him an angel from heaven, strengthening him. And being in an agony, he prayed the longer. And his sweat became as drops of blood, trickling down upon the ground." Look at the order. The angel comes, and the agony deepens. The angel doesn't take the cup away; the angel helps him drink it. In Luke's picture, strength from heaven isn't an exit. It's company in it. Agony, in Luke's Greek, is agonia, a word that could describe an athlete's strain before a contest, as well as deep anguish. And the sweat is as drops of blood: like. Readers have long debated whether Luke means real blood or heavy, dark drops; the text doesn't settle it. Some early manuscripts of Luke don't have these two verses. The Church receives them as Scripture, and they're in the Latin Vulgate and the Douay. And the disciples? He finds them sleeping for sorrow. Luke is gentle: grief knocked them out. Catholics pray this moment as the first sorrowful mystery of the rosary, the Agony in the Garden, and some keep a holy hour, remembering that in Matthew and Mark, Jesus asks his friends to watch one hour with him.

482.title: The servant's ear (Luke 22:47–53)
482.hook: even while arrested he heals the ear Peter cut off
482.howItsDone: Catholics hear the arrest in the garden in the Passion read on Palm Sunday and Good Friday, and the healing of the servant's ear is preached by many as Christ's refusal of violence even in his own defense.

segments.voice: Yesterday, agonia: sweat like drops of blood, and an angel who strengthened him. Your line was an angel strengthened him.

The prayer in the garden is over. Torches come up the hill: a crowd with swords and clubs, and at the front a familiar face, Judas, one of the twelve, leaning in to kiss his teacher. In the dark it happens fast. Someone near Jesus asks, Lord, shall we strike with the sword? and doesn't wait for the answer. A blade swings. The servant of the high priest is holding the side of his head; his right ear is gone. What Jesus does next is the last healing Luke records before the cross.
screen: `TORCHES IN THE GARDEN.` → `A KISS, THEN A SWORD.` → `A RIGHT EAR CUT OFF.`

segments.voice: All four Gospels tell of the sword in the garden. Only John gives the names: the one with the sword is Simon Peter, and the servant is Malchus. Only Luke, the doctor's Gospel by old tradition, tells what happened next: "But Jesus answering, said: Suffer ye thus far. And when he had touched his ear, he healed him." Suffer ye thus far is an old phrase, and nobody is fully sure of the Greek's exact sense. Many modern readers hear no more of this: enough, stop here. Others hear Jesus speaking to the crowd: let me go this far, let me reach him. Either way, the fighting ends with a hand on a stranger's wound. Look who gets healed: not a friend or a disciple, but a man who came out at night to arrest him. And look when: Jesus is about to be bound, and his own hands are still free to touch. Then he tells the chief priests and captains plainly that they could have taken him any day in the temple, "but this is your hour, and the power of darkness." He names the darkness and doesn't fight it with a sword. He refuses violence, and he repairs what his own side broke. Peter swung the blade; Jesus cleans up after Peter. Most of the damage we have to mend wasn't done by our enemies. It was done by us, or by people on our side, trying to help.

Picture what touching it would look like: a message, an apology with no excuse attached, fixing the thing. If you pray, ask for the nerve to mend it; if not, just hold it in front of you and choose one small next step.

483.title: Herod's mockery (Luke 23:6–12)
483.hook: Herod wants a show, gets silence, and he and Pilate become friends
483.howItsDone: Catholics hear Luke's account of Jesus before Herod in the Passion read on Palm Sunday in the year of Luke, and his silence is sometimes linked in preaching with the suffering servant of Isaiah 53.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Malchus: a sword in the garden, and a hand that healed the man who came to arrest him. Your line was no more of this.

Early morning in Jerusalem. Pilate, the Roman governor, has a prisoner he doesn't want. Then someone mentions that the man is from Galilee. Galilee belongs to Herod Antipas, and Luke says Herod is in Jerusalem in those days. Pilate sees a way out: send him over. So Jesus is walked across town to a different palace and a different ruler, the son of the Herod from the Christmas story. And this Herod is delighted. He has wanted to meet this man for a long time. Not to listen. To be entertained.
screen: `PILATE PASSES THE PROBLEM.` → `HEROD IS DELIGHTED.` → `HE WANTS A SHOW.`

segments.voice: Only Luke tells this scene, and he says what Herod was after: he hoped to see some sign done by him. A miracle, on demand, for the court. So Herod questions him at length. And then, in the Douay-Rheims: "But he answered him nothing." Remember who Herod is: the ruler who had John the Baptist beheaded. Earlier in Luke, Jesus calls him that fox. Now the fox has him in the room, and Jesus won't perform. The chief priests stand nearby shouting accusations. Herod and his soldiers, getting no reaction, turn to mockery. They treat him with contempt and send him back, the Douay says, "putting on him a white garment." A costume. A joke about a king. Then a strange, quiet sentence: Herod and Pilate became friends that same day, though before they had been enemies. Two rulers who couldn't stand each other found common ground in a prisoner they both refused to take seriously. Some readers hear in this silence Isaiah's suffering servant, who opened not his mouth. It isn't sulking, and it isn't weakness. It's a refusal to turn the holiest things into a party trick for someone who only wants to watch. Someone often wants a performance from us: the clever comeback, the outrage, the show for the audience. Silence before Herod is a way of saying, I won't play that part.
screen: `HEROD HOPED TO SEE A SIGN.` · `BUT HE ANSWERED HIM NOTHING.` · `A WHITE GARMENT, A JOKE OF A KING.` · `ENEMIES BECOME FRIENDS THAT DAY.`

segments.voice: Think of a place where you put on a show: a meeting where you try to sound clever, a feed where you post for applause, a relative who always gets the version of you they expect. Picture yourself there, quieter, not cold or sulking, just declining the act, with nothing to prove. If you pray, bring that place to God and ask to be the same person in it.
Herod's mockery. A ruler who wanted a miracle for entertainment, got silence, and dressed Jesus up as a joke. Today's word.
Your line: silence before Herod. And that's week sixty-nine: he wept over the city, mites, do this, diakonon, drops of blood, Malchus, and Herod.
